title: Subquery vs Join
description: Compare SQL subqueries and joins by result grain, duplicates, NULLs, scalar cardinality and measured optimizer behavior, with equivalent and unsafe rewrites.
notes:
## Choose the result you mean before choosing syntax

A subquery is a query nested inside another SQL statement. A join combines rows from table expressions according to a relationship or condition. They often express related tasks, but replacing one with the other is correct only when the required rows, duplicates, null handling and missing-match behavior remain the same. A shorter query is not automatically a better query, and a familiar join is not automatically faster.

Imagine a training center listing instructors who have at least one confirmed session. The result should contain one row per instructor, regardless of how many sessions that instructor teaches. That is an existence question. Another report needs every instructor-session pair, including the session date. That is a matching-row question. These reports start from the same tables while asking for different result grains.

## Compare an existence filter with a matching join

Use this small fixture to make the difference visible. Instructor one has two confirmed sessions, instructor two has one cancelled session, and instructor three has none. Assume instructor_id is the instructors primary key and session_id identifies each session. A nullable foreign key in the session table would not match an instructor under ordinary equality.

```sql
CREATE TABLE instructors(instructor_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(40));
CREATE TABLE sessions(session_id INT PRIMARY KEY, instructor_id INT, status VARCHAR(12));
INSERT INTO instructors VALUES (1,'Mira'),(2,'Jon'),(3,'Asha');
INSERT INTO sessions VALUES (10,1,'confirmed'),(11,1,'confirmed'),(12,2,'cancelled');
SELECT i.instructor_id, i.name
FROM instructors i
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sessions s
              WHERE s.instructor_id=i.instructor_id AND s.status='confirmed')
ORDER BY i.instructor_id;
```

The result is one row for Mira. EXISTS asks whether the correlated query returns any qualifying row; it does not append the session rows to the output. Selecting the constant one communicates that the payload is irrelevant. It does not mean only one session is examined, nor does it promise a specific physical loop or access method.

An inner join with the same matching condition produces two Mira rows when only instructor columns are projected. Those are separate matching pairs, even though the displayed values look identical. DISTINCT can collapse the projected duplicates, but that additional instruction should reflect the report's intended semantics. Selecting session_id would make the two rows distinct again. Do not apply DISTINCT as a universal repair for an incorrectly chosen result grain.

## Preserve the right identity when deduplicating

Suppose two instructors share the name Mira. Projecting only name and adding DISTINCT merges different people into one displayed row. An EXISTS filter preserves the number of outer rows; it does not repair a nonunique outer input or prevent a later projection from concealing identities. Include the stable identifier when the requirement distinguishes people rather than names.

A join rewrite can also change aggregate results. Counting instructor rows after joining sessions counts pairs, while counting instructors before that multiplication counts instructors. COUNT(DISTINCT instructor_id) can express the latter on a joined relation when appropriate, but its null and grouping behavior still needs inspection. Write expected output on a fixture containing multiple matches and repeated display names before deciding that two forms are equivalent.

## Express absence with an explicit missing-match contract

NOT EXISTS returns an outer instructor when no qualifying confirmed session exists. A left anti-join can express the same result by putting the complete qualifying condition in ON and testing a guaranteed nonnull right-side identifier for null afterward. Testing a nullable descriptive attribute can wrongly classify a real matched row as missing.

```sql
SELECT i.instructor_id
FROM instructors i
LEFT JOIN sessions s
  ON s.instructor_id=i.instructor_id AND s.status='confirmed'
WHERE s.session_id IS NULL
ORDER BY i.instructor_id;
```

This returns instructors two and three. Moving the confirmed-status condition from ON into WHERE changes what happens to null-extended rows and can remove the very missing matches the report intends to keep. NOT IN introduces another issue when its subquery can return null: an unknown comparison can prevent expected rows from passing. Prove nullability or use the absence form whose meaning matches the requirement.

## Treat scalar subqueries as a different shape

A scalar subquery supplies one value rather than a collection of joined rows. It must return at most one row; zero rows yield null, and more than one row is an error in MySQL. Rewriting it as an unrestricted join can silently multiply rows instead of preserving that error contract. A unique constraint can make a one-row relationship explicit; current sample uniqueness cannot substitute for that constraint.

An aggregate scalar subquery without GROUP BY returns one aggregate row even when no input matches. COUNT then gives zero, whereas SUM normally gives null. A grouped derived table left joined to instructors has no group for an instructor with no sessions, so its count column becomes null after null extension. COALESCE may be required to preserve the original zero, but only where zero is the intended business meaning.

## Preaggregate at the required comparison level

For a report of sessions longer than their instructor's average duration, a correlated aggregate can state the comparison directly. A second form groups sessions by instructor once as a logical table expression, then joins the averages to individual sessions. Both must use the same population, status filter and null handling. Filtering cancelled sessions in only one form changes the denominator and invalidates the comparison.

The grouped form makes the intermediate grain explicit: one average per instructor. However, saying it is computed once describes the relational formulation, not a guarantee about execution. An optimizer may merge, materialize, decorrelate or otherwise transform eligible expressions. Keep the readable logical explanation distinct from claims about how many physical scans occurred.

## Measure plans on representative data

MySQL can transform eligible subqueries using semijoin, materialization and other strategies. Joins and subqueries can therefore converge on similar execution work. Conversely, a correlated expression that cannot be transformed may perform repeated work. Neither observation establishes that every correlated subquery is slow or that every join is optimal.

Use EXPLAIN to inspect a plan and an appropriate measured execution facility in a controlled environment when actual timings are needed. Include realistic row counts, value distribution, indexes and parameters. A plan on twelve warm-cache rows cannot establish production behavior on skewed millions. Separate query correctness from tuning evidence; a fast query with the wrong duplicate behavior still fails the task.

## Keep qualification and projection separate

A derived table in FROM can expose several columns and rows, unlike a scalar expression. Give it an alias and inspect whether its grouping keys are unique before joining. If the derived relation contains two rows per instructor, joining it restores the same multiplication that an existence filter avoided. Parentheses alone do not create uniqueness, and an ORDER BY inside a derived expression does not promise final report ordering.

Apply the same care to null-safe equality. Replacing ordinary equality with a null-safe comparison changes whether two unknown keys are considered a match. That can be useful under an explicitly chosen rule, but it is not a harmless performance rewrite. Check collation and type conversion too when one form introduces casts or differently typed comparison columns. A defensible rewrite keeps these comparison semantics visible instead of relying on convenient test values.

## Solve two rewrites and challenge the boundaries

For a beginner exercise, return instructor identifiers having any session, using EXISTS. The solution retains instructors one and two exactly once. Add a second session for instructor two and verify that the result cardinality stays two. Then write the equivalent join-and-distinct form retaining the identifier, and explain why the raw join has extra rows.

For an intermediate exercise, return instructors with no confirmed sessions using both NOT EXISTS and the left anti-join above. Add a session with a null instructor key and another cancelled session for instructor one. The result remains instructors two and three because neither addition creates a confirmed relationship for them. An empty instructor table must produce an empty result, while an empty session table includes every instructor.

A useful final comparison records output columns, one-row identity, duplicate rules, null rules and missing-match rules before considering execution cost. Continue with [EXISTS](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/exists), [semi joins](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/semi-join), [scalar subqueries](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/scalar-subquery) and [join cardinality](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/join-cardinality). Choose the clearest correct expression, then measure the implementation that will actually run it.

questions.question_text: Which principle avoids a misleading blanket speed claim about joins and subqueries?
options: Joins are always faster, no exceptions
Equivalent forms can share optimizer strategies; compare measured plans and correct results.
They can never produce the same result
questions.explanation: Syntax alone does not determine the execution strategy.

questions.question_text: Why can a JOIN+DISTINCT version of "which departments have employees" be less ideal than EXISTS?
options: JOIN cannot be used with the departments/employees tables
The join can produce one row per matching employee, requiring DISTINCT to clean up duplicates that EXISTS never creates
EXISTS is always a syntax error
JOIN always returns fewer rows than EXISTS
questions.explanation: A join multiplies rows per match, needing DISTINCT to dedupe, whereas EXISTS is a pure yes/no test.

questions.question_text: What is the JOIN-only equivalent trick for NOT EXISTS?
options: LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right_table.key IS NULL
questions.explanation: The classic anti-join pattern finds unmatched left rows via a LEFT JOIN plus an IS NULL filter.

questions.question_text: What is a "hidden performance trap at scale" mentioned for subqueries in SELECT?
options: A correlated scalar subquery in SELECT can force per-row re-evaluation, unlike a window function or joined pre-aggregate
They cannot be combined with WHERE
questions.explanation: This callback to 17.9 highlights the per-row cost of correlated SELECT subqueries at scale.

questions.question_text: At the logical query level, what does the joined preaggregate for above-department-average comparisons make explicit?
options: A derived relation with one grouped average per department, joined to employee rows; actual physical work remains optimizer-dependent
It requires a scalar subquery still
questions.explanation: The grouped formulation exposes the intermediate grain. It does not guarantee one physical computation or prove that a correlated form cannot be transformed.

questions.question_text: Which subquery type is often considered clearer than an equivalent join for "does a match exist" questions?
questions.explanation: EXISTS directly expresses "does a related row exist" without needing a join plus DISTINCT.

questions.question_text: Which statement about row counts is accurate?
options: A WHERE-clause subquery can multiply outer rows just like a JOIN can
A WHERE-clause subquery only filters the outer row set; it never multiplies rows the way a JOIN can
Subqueries and joins always produce identical row counts
questions.explanation: Subqueries used as WHERE filters can only include or exclude outer rows, never duplicate them.

questions.question_text: What is the recommended general approach when deciding between a subquery and a join?
options: Consider the specific question, likely optimizer behavior, and readability — measure rather than assume one is universally better
questions.explanation: There's no universal winner; the right choice depends on the query's intent, the optimizer, and clarity.

questions.question_text: An instructor has three matching sessions. How many outer rows does EXISTS retain for that instructor?
options: One when the outer input contains one row for that identity
questions.explanation: EXISTS filters an outer row without producing one result per child match.

questions.question_text: Why can SELECT DISTINCT name merge two different instructors?
options: Names can repeat across distinct identities
questions.explanation: Deduplicating a projection loses distinctions omitted from that projection.

questions.question_text: Which right-side column is suitable for the anti-join IS NULL test here?
questions.explanation: A matched session cannot have a null primary key.

questions.question_text: Where does the confirmed-status condition belong in the displayed anti-join?
questions.explanation: ON determines which qualifying matches prevent null extension.

questions.question_text: What does a zero-row scalar subquery yield?
questions.explanation: The scalar expression has no value row and evaluates to null.

questions.question_text: What does a multirow scalar subquery cause in MySQL?
options: Implicit choice of the first row
questions.explanation: A scalar expression cannot supply several rows.

questions.question_text: What can a join rewrite accidentally change?
questions.explanation: Logical equivalence requires more than similar-looking predicates.

questions.question_text: An aggregate COUNT subquery gives zero for no sessions. A left joined grouped count gives NULL. What should the rewrite consider?
options: Replacing every missing value with one
COALESCE to zero when zero preserves the intended meaning
questions.explanation: No grouped child row differs from an aggregate row containing zero.

questions.question_text: Does a correlated SQL spelling prove per-row physical execution?
options: No; eligible expressions can be transformed
Only when aliases have one character
questions.explanation: Optimizer transformations separate logical syntax from physical execution.

questions.question_text: What is needed before comparing the speed of two forms?
questions.explanation: A faster answer to a different question is not a valid optimization.

questions.question_text: What happens to NOT IN when nullable subquery values introduce UNKNOWN?
options: The query becomes a left join automatically
Expected nonmatches can fail the WHERE filter
All outer rows are guaranteed to pass
questions.explanation: WHERE retains true, not unknown.

questions.question_text: Which evidence best supports a performance conclusion?
options: Representative plans and measured execution under documented conditions
questions.explanation: Workload, indexes, distributions and runtime conditions affect the result.
